module_title: Specific Fruit Juices: Citrus and Orchard Fruits

lessons.title: Orange and Grapefruit Juice Production
lessons.body:
To make fresh orange or grapefruit juice, start with ripe fruit. For oranges, choose varieties like Valencia or Navel. For grapefruit, pick Ruby Red or Marsh. In Africa, citrus grows well in Kenya, South Africa, and Nigeria. Harvest in the morning when fruit is cool. Wash fruit in clean water with a little salt to remove dirt and pests. You will need a sharp knife, cutting board, manual or electric citrus juicer, clean buckets, muslin cloth, and bottles. For a small batch, 10 oranges yield about 1 litre of juice. Grapefruit yields slightly less due to thicker skin.

Cut fruit in half. If using a manual juicer, press and twist each half. For electric juicers, follow the manufacturer's instructions. Strain juice through muslin cloth to remove seeds and pulp. For clear juice, let it settle for 30 minutes, then siphon off the top. You can add sugar to taste, but start with 1 tablespoon per litre. For preservation, heat juice to 85Â°C for 15 minutes (pasteurisation), then pour hot into sterilised bottles. Seal immediately. This extends shelf life to 3 months in a cool, dark place. Without pasteurisation, keep refrigerated and drink within 3 days.

For a business, scale up. Use a stainless steel pot for heating. Avoid aluminium as it reacts with acid. Test acidity with a pH meter or litmus paper; target pH 3.5 or lower for safety. Add 0.1% ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to prevent browning. Bottle in clean glass or PET bottles. Label with production date. Sell fresh juice to local shops, schools, or at markets. In Kenya, a litre of fresh orange juice sells for 300-500 KES. Ensure hygiene: wash hands, sterilise equipment with boiling water, and keep flies away. This simple process can become a profitable micro-business.

lessons.title: Apple Cider and Clear Apple Juice Making
lessons.body:
Apple juice is popular worldwide. In Africa, apples grow in South Africa, Morocco, and Kenya (highlands). For juice, use sweet-tart apples like Granny Smith or Fuji. You need a fruit press or a strong blender, muslin cloth, large pot, and bottles. Start with 5 kg of apples to make about 2 litres of juice. Wash apples, remove stems and rotten spots. Do not peel or core if you want more flavour, but remove seeds as they contain small amounts of cyanide. Cut into quarters.

For clear apple juice, crush apples into a pulp using a blender or grater. Wrap pulp in muslin cloth and squeeze hard to extract juice. For cider, simply press and let juice ferment naturally. To make clear juice, heat extracted juice to 80Â°C for 10 minutes. This stops enzymes that cause cloudiness. Then cool quickly and strain through a fine cloth or coffee filter. You can add pectinase enzyme (available in brewing shops) to break down pectin and improve clarity. Let it settle overnight, then siphon off clear juice. Pasteurise at 85Â°C for 15 minutes and bottle hot.

For apple cider, allow fresh juice to ferment in a clean container with an airlock for 1-2 weeks. Wild yeasts on apple skins will start fermentation. For a stronger cider, add wine yeast. After fermentation, siphon off sediment and bottle. Cider can be drunk still or sparkling. In Africa, apple cider is less common but can be a niche product. Sell clear apple juice as a healthy drink. Ensure all equipment is sterilised with boiling water. Store bottles in a cool, dark place. Shelf life for pasteurised juice is 6 months; cider can last a year if sealed properly. Start small, test your product, and scale up.

lessons.title: Grape Juice: From Concord to Muscadine
lessons.body:
Grapes grow in many African countries, including South Africa, Egypt, and Morocco. For juice, Concord grapes are ideal for their rich flavour, but Muscadine grapes are also good. You need ripe, sweet grapes. Wash them well. Remove stems and any spoiled grapes. You can leave skins on for red juice or peel for white juice. A steam juicer is best, but you can use a large pot and muslin cloth. For 2 kg of grapes, you get about 1.5 litres of juice.

Crush grapes lightly to release juice. For clear juice, heat crushed grapes to 70Â°C for 10 minutes, then strain through muslin. For a more intense flavour, simmer for 20 minutes. Add sugar to taste: about 1 cup per 4 litres of juice. For Concord, you may need less sugar due to natural sweetness. Muscadine grapes have thick skins and seeds; strain well. You can also make grape juice by cold-pressing. After extracting, pasteurise at 85Â°C for 15 minutes. Bottle hot into sterilised bottles. For sparkling grape juice, add a little yeast and bottle in strong bottles, but be careful of explosions.

In Africa, grape juice is a premium product. Sell fresh or pasteurised. For a business, consider blending with other fruits like apple or pineapple. Store in a cool, dark place. Pasteurised juice lasts 6 months. Unpasteurised juice must be refrigerated and consumed within 3 days. Always test pH: grape juice should be around 3.3-3.5. Add 0.1% ascorbic acid to prevent browning. Label bottles with date and ingredients. Market to health-conscious consumers. You can also make grape jelly from the pulp. Start with 10 kg of grapes to test the market.

lessons.title: Pineapple and Tropical Fruit Juices
lessons.body:
Pineapple juice is a favourite in Africa, where pineapple grows abundantly in Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, and Tanzania. Use ripe pineapples with a sweet aroma. You need a sharp knife, blender or juicer, muslin cloth, pot, and bottles. One large pineapple yields about 500 ml of juice. Peel the pineapple, remove eyes, and cut into chunks. Blend or juice. Strain through muslin for clear juice, or leave pulp for a thicker juice. Add water if too strong: 1 part water to 3 parts juice. Sugar to taste, but pineapple is already sweet. For a tropical blend, mix with mango, passion fruit, or guava. For mango juice, use ripe mangoes, peel and blend, strain. Passion fruit: scoop seeds and pulp, blend briefly, strain. Guava: wash, cut, blend, strain.

Pasteurise juice at 85Â°C for 15 minutes to extend shelf life. For fresh sale, keep refrigerated. Add 0.1% ascorbic acid to prevent browning. For pineapple, you can also add a pinch of salt to enhance sweetness. In Africa, fresh pineapple juice is sold in markets and bars. A litre sells for 200-400 KES. For a business, invest in a good juicer and stainless steel pots. Avoid aluminium. Sterilise bottles with boiling water. For tropical blends, combine 50% pineapple, 30% mango, and 20% passion fruit for a delicious mix. Label with date and ingredients. Store in cool, dark place. Pasteurised juice lasts 3 months. Unpasteurised lasts 3 days refrigerated. Start with 10 pineapples to test. You can also freeze juice in plastic bags for longer storage.

lessons.title: Berry Juices: Strawberry, Blueberry, and Raspberry
lessons.body:
Berries are not as common in Africa, but strawberries grow in Kenya, Egypt, and South Africa. Blueberries and raspberries are less common but can be imported or grown in cooler highlands. For juice, use ripe, firm berries. Wash gently. Remove stems and leaves. You need a blender, muslin cloth, pot, and bottles. For 500g of strawberries, you get about 300 ml of juice. Blueberries yield similar. Raspberries are more delicate; handle carefully. Blend berries with a little water (1 cup per 500g) to help extraction. Strain through muslin. For clear juice, let it settle and siphon off top. For a thicker juice, skip straining.

Berry juices are often tart, so add sugar to taste: start with 2 tablespoons per 500 ml. You can also mix with apple or grape juice for sweetness. Pasteurise at 85Â°C for 15 minutes. Add 0.1% ascorbic acid to preserve colour and vitamin C. For strawberry juice, you can add a squeeze of lemon to brighten flavour. For blueberry, a pinch of cinnamon enhances taste. For raspberry, strain well to remove seeds. In Africa, berry juices are premium. Sell fresh or pasteurised. A 250 ml bottle can sell for 150-300 KES. For a business, focus on quality and hygiene. Sterilise all equipment. Store pasteurised juice in cool, dark place for up to 6 months. Unpasteurised juice must be refrigerated and consumed within 2 days. You can also make berry smoothies by blending with yoghurt. Start with 1 kg of berries to test market. Label with date and ingredients.

lessons.title: Stone Fruit Juices: Peach, Plum, and Cherry
lessons.body:
Stone fruits like peaches, plums, and cherries grow in South Africa, Morocco, and Egypt. For juice, use ripe, soft fruit. Wash well. Remove pits (stones) as they contain toxins. You need a knife, blender, muslin cloth, pot, and bottles. For 1 kg of peaches, you get about 700 ml of juice. Plums yield similar. Cherries yield less, about 500 ml per kg. Cut fruit into pieces, remove pits. Blend with a little water (1 cup per kg) to aid extraction. Strain through muslin for clear juice. For a thicker juice, leave some pulp. Peaches and plums have natural sweetness; cherries are tart. Add sugar to taste: 1-2 tablespoons per litre. For cherry juice, you may need more sugar.

Pasteurise at 85Â°C for 15 minutes. Add 0.1% ascorbic acid to prevent browning. For peach juice, a dash of lemon juice enhances flavour. For plum juice, a pinch of ginger adds zing. For cherry juice, a little almond extract can complement. In Africa, stone fruit juices are less common but can be a niche product. Sell fresh or pasteurised. A litre of peach juice sells for 300-500 KES. For a business, ensure you remove all pits. Sterilise bottles and equipment. Store pasteurised juice in cool, dark place for 6 months. Unpasteurised juice lasts 3 days refrigerated. You can blend stone fruits with apple or grape juice for a balanced flavour. Start with 5 kg of fruit to test. Label with date and ingredients. Consider making jams from leftover pulp.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Citrus and Orchard Fruit Juice Production

This practical reference consolidates the technical parameters, yield expectations, and safety thresholds that determine whether a fruit juice enterprise in Africa moves from subsistence processing to a commercially viable, repeatable business. The focus here is on citrus (orange and grapefruit) and orchard fruits (apple, grape, pineapple, berry, and stone fruits). The numbers below are drawn from FAO, USDA, and peer-reviewed food science sources, and are presented in a business-first format: every figure is tied to a decision you will make on the processing floor.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, fruit juice processing is one of the highest-margin agro-processing opportunities available to small and medium enterprises. Post-harvest losses for fruits in the region routinely exceed 30â40% (FAO, 2019), which means raw material is often cheap and abundant during harvest windows. The constraint is not fruit supply â it is consistent extraction, preservation, and packaging that meets food safety standards. This module gives you the reference data to solve that constraint.

Table 1: Extraction Yield, Brix, and pH Reference by Fruit

Fruit Juice Yield (L/100 kg) Typical Brix (Â°Bx) pH Key Process Note
Orange (Valencia)45â5510â123.5â4.0Ream or press; avoid oil from peel (bitterness)
Grapefruit40â509â113.0â3.5Remove naringin-heavy albedo to reduce bitterness
Apple (clear)60â7011â133.3â3.8Enzyme treatment + fining for clarity
Apple (cloudy/cider)70â7511â143.3â3.8Rapid pressing, minimal oxidation
Grape (Concord)60â7014â183.0â3.5Hot-press for color and tannin extraction
Grape (Muscadine)55â6513â163.0â3.4Cold-press; high antioxidant, low acid
Pineapple50â6011â143.3â3.8Peel & core removal; bromelain inactivation by heat

Sources: FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (1995); USDA National Nutrient Database; Bates et al., Journal of Food Science (2001); Ashurst, Chemistry and Technology of Soft Drinks and Fruit Juices (2016).

Table 2: Preservation and Shelf-Life Parameters

Method Temperature / Dose Hold Time Shelf Life (unopened) Equipment Level
Hot-fill pasteurisation88â95Â°C15â30 sec6â12 monthsLowâmedium
Flash pasteurisation72â75Â°C15â20 sec3â6 months (chilled)Medium
Thermal (in-bottle)80â85Â°C20â30 min6â12 monthsLow
Refrigeration only0â4Â°Câ5â14 daysVery low
Chemical (benzoate/sorbate)0.05â0.1%â3â6 monthsLow
Frozen concentrateâ18Â°Câ12â24 monthsMedium

Sources: FDA, Juice HACCP Hazards and Controls Guidance (2023); FAO, Small-Scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing (1997); Codex Alimentarius CAC/RCP 1-1969 (Rev. 2020).

â  SAFETY WARNING â CRITICAL CONTROL POINTS

1. Pasteurisation is non-negotiable. Unpasteurised juice is a known vehicle for E. coli O157:H7, Salmonella, and Cryptosporidium. In Africa, where cold-chain reliability varies, hot-fill at 88â95Â°C for 15â30 seconds is the minimum safe standard. Never sell raw juice to the public.

2. Water quality. If you dilute juice or wash fruit, use potable water only. Contaminated wash water cross-contaminates the entire batch. Chlorinate wash water at 50â100 ppm free chlorine and test daily.

3. Mycotoxins in apple and grape. Patulin (apple) and ochratoxin A (grape) are heat-stable. Reject mouldy fruit at receiving â pasteurisation will NOT destroy these toxins.

4. Allergen and additive labelling. Declare preservatives (E211, E202) and sulphites on the label. Sulphites above 10 ppm must be declared â failure is a legal liability and a trade barrier for export.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Receiving: Reject mouldy, bruised, or over-ripe fruit. Weigh and record every batch. Mouldy fruit = mycotoxin risk, not just quality loss.
  2. Wash and sort: Use potable water with 50â100 ppm chlorine. Remove leaves, stems, stones, and foreign matter before extraction.
  3. Extraction: Match the method to the fruit â ream citrus, press orchard fruit, mill pineapple. Avoid excessive peel contact (bitterness, oil).
  4. Brix and pH: Measure every batch with a refractometer and pH meter. Adjust with sugar or citric acid to hit your product specification before pasteurisation.
  5. Pasteurise: Hot-fill at 88â95Â°C for 15â30 seconds. Record temperature and time for every batch. No record = no proof of safety.
  6. Fill and cap: Fill hot (â¥85Â°C) into pre-sterilised bottles. Cap immediately. Invert for 30 seconds to sterilise the headspace and cap.
  7. Cool and label: Cool rapidly in a water bath to below 40Â°C. Label with batch number, date, ingredients, and allergen declarations.
  8. Store and sell: Keep in a cool, dark room. Use FIFO (first-in, first-out). Never sell a batch without a pasteurisation record.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 119) â free full text, covers extraction, preservation, and small-scale enterprise setup.
  • FDA â Juice HACCP Hazards and Controls Guidance â the global benchmark for juice safety, free to download.
  • FAO â Small-Scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing â practical equipment and layout guidance for African SMEs.
  • Codex Alimentarius â General Principles of Food Hygiene (CAC/RCP 1-1969) â the international food safety baseline.
  • USDA Agricultural Research Service â Fruit and Juice Composition Data â free compositional data for product formulation.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. All figures are indicative and should be validated with local raw material testing before commercial production. Always comply with your national food safety authority (e.g., NAFDAC in Nigeria, KEBS in Kenya, SABS in South Africa).

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH level for safe citrus juice?
quiz.explanation: Low pH (3.5 or lower) inhibits harmful bacteria growth in citrus juice.

quiz.q: How many oranges are needed to make approximately 1 litre of juice?
quiz.explanation: About 10 oranges yield 1 litre of juice, depending on size and juicing method.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of pasteurising juice at 85Â°C for 15 minutes?
options: B) To kill microbes and extend shelf life
quiz.explanation: Pasteurisation kills spoilage organisms and pathogens, extending shelf life.

quiz.q: Which apple variety is recommended for making juice?
quiz.explanation: Granny Smith is a sweet-tart apple ideal for juice, but other varieties can also be used.

quiz.q: Why should apple seeds be removed before juicing?
options: D) They add too much sugar
quiz.explanation: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide when crushed.

quiz.q: What enzyme can be added to apple juice to improve clarity?
quiz.explanation: Pectinase breaks down pectin, which causes cloudiness in apple juice.

quiz.q: How long should apple cider ferment naturally?
quiz.explanation: Natural fermentation of apple cider takes about 1-2 weeks with wild yeasts.

quiz.q: Which grape variety is known for rich flavour in juice?
quiz.explanation: Concord grapes are prized for their intense, sweet flavour in juice.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of juice from 2 kg of grapes?
quiz.explanation: 2 kg of grapes typically yield about 1.5 litres of juice.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid aluminium pots when making grape juice?
options: D) They are hard to clean
quiz.explanation: Aluminium reacts with acidic juice, leaching metal and affecting taste.

quiz.q: Which tropical fruit is a common base for juice in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Pineapple grows abundantly in Africa and is widely used for juice.

quiz.q: How much juice does one large pineapple yield?
quiz.explanation: A large pineapple yields about 500 ml of juice.

quiz.q: What can be added to pineapple juice to enhance sweetness?
quiz.explanation: A pinch of salt can enhance the natural sweetness of pineapple juice.

quiz.q: Which tropical fruit blend is suggested in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends a blend of 50% pineapple, 30% mango, and 20% passion fruit.

quiz.q: How long does unpasteurised tropical juice last in the refrigerator?
quiz.explanation: Unpasteurised juice should be refrigerated and consumed within 3 days.

quiz.q: Which berry is most commonly grown in Africa for juice?
quiz.explanation: Strawberries are grown in Kenya, Egypt, and South Africa, unlike many other berries.

quiz.q: How much juice can you get from 500g of strawberries?
quiz.explanation: 500g of strawberries yield about 300 ml of juice.

quiz.q: What should be added to berry juice to preserve colour and vitamin C?
quiz.explanation: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) prevents oxidation and preserves colour and nutrients.

quiz.q: Which spice can enhance blueberry juice?
quiz.explanation: A pinch of cinnamon complements the flavour of blueberry juice.

quiz.q: How long does pasteurised berry juice last in a cool, dark place?
quiz.explanation: Pasteurised berry juice can last up to 6 months if stored properly.

quiz.q: Which stone fruit is a good source of juice in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Peaches grow in South Africa, Morocco, and Egypt and are used for juice.

quiz.q: Why must pits be removed from stone fruits before juicing?
quiz.explanation: Stone fruit pits contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide.

quiz.q: How much juice can you get from 1 kg of peaches?
quiz.explanation: 1 kg of peaches yields about 700 ml of juice.

quiz.q: What can be added to peach juice to enhance flavour?
quiz.explanation: A dash of lemon juice brightens the flavour of peach juice.

quiz.q: Which stone fruit juice is naturally tart and may need more sugar?
quiz.explanation: Cherries are tart, so cherry juice often requires additional sugar.

quiz.q: What is a recommended storage time for unpasteurised stone fruit juice?
quiz.explanation: Unpasteurised stone fruit juice should be consumed within 3 days if refrigerated.

quiz.q: What can be made from leftover stone fruit pulp?
quiz.explanation: Leftover pulp can be cooked with sugar to make jam.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key hygiene practice when making juice?
options: A) Sterilise bottles with boiling water
B) Use the same cloth for all fruits
quiz.explanation: Sterilising bottles prevents contamination and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pasteurisation temperature for fruit juice?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 85Â°C for 15 minutes is sufficient to pasteurise juice without degrading quality.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label juice bottles with production date?
options: B) To track shelf life and safety
quiz.explanation: Date labels help consumers know when the juice is no longer safe to drink.
